name: "content-briefing"

# Content briefing

## Goal
Turn an agreed content opportunity into a shared understanding of the page we want to make. A useful brief gives the writer direction and lets the owner correct the angle before time goes into drafting.

## Suggested approach
Read the relevant business or website context, research and existing content. Understand the reader's question and why this page would help. Check whether the task is a new page or an improvement to an existing one.

Develop the proposed angle, intended reader, main answer and distinctive contribution. Suggest an outline when it helps explain the approach, without prescribing every paragraph. Consider examples, product demonstrations or other evidence that will make the page convincing, along with useful links and a natural next step for the reader.

Adapt this to the page type and the owner's goals. A tutorial needs a working procedure; a comparison needs fair decision criteria; a personal or creative site may need a different treatment. Consult the relevant existing article playbook rather than imposing one format on all work.

Discuss missing information that would materially change the brief. Bring a concrete proposal to the owner and improve it through their feedback, rather than asking them to supply the entire assignment.

This workflow's brief approval still requires the user question, target query, intent, observed demand evidence, product fit, required proof, conversion path and owner. Explain these in language appropriate to the site; for a non-commercial project, fit and the next visitor action should reflect its purpose. Do not invent evidence to fill a field. Obtain owner approval of the actual brief before drafting.

## A useful brief format
Use this as a readable starting shape, not a form to fill mechanically. Keep the existing record metadata separate from the editorial proposal. A small update may need a short note; a new comparison usually needs more detail.

### Proposal
Give a working title, page type and whether this creates a page or updates an existing URL. In a short paragraph explain who the reader is, what they are trying to do, the main answer we intend to give, why this site can help and what this piece adds. State important boundaries so the writer knows what not to cover. Suggest a few genuinely different title/angle options only when a choice would help; recommend one.

### Search and audience evidence
Name the target query, intended search intent and linked observed demand. Summarize representative current results and what they suggest about format, depth and unmet needs, with date/locale and capture limitations. Reuse planning research; refresh it when stale or when the angle changes. Keep related questions together when they support the same task rather than making a keyword quota. Explain how the proposal differs from existing site pages.

### Proposed structure
Give descriptive section headings with a sentence about the question each section answers. Note the key example, demonstration, comparison or source that belongs there. A heading list alone is often too vague; a nearly complete draft defeats the purpose of brief approval. Sequence the reader's questions rather than copying competitors' headings.

### Proof and assets
Connect consequential claims to available sources or planned verification. For example: 'Setup takes these steps: verify by running the documented workflow'; 'Supports private deployment: confirm current deployment documentation'; 'Saves time: needs a defined measurement, otherwise omit the quantified promise.' Distinguish evidence already held from work still required. Name needed screenshots, diagrams, datasets, interviews or runnable examples, what each should show, and any owner-supplied material. A planned test is not a passed test.

### Reader journey and decisions
Suggest useful existing internal links and a natural next action, such as trying the procedure, downloading a resource or reading the next guide. Include the owner and a short batch of decisions needed about angle, scope or proof. Make your recommendation first. Clearly state what is ready for approval and what missing evidence prevents it. Do not treat a casual topic selection as approval of this brief.

## Format-specific starting points
- **Tutorial:** promised outcome, audience prerequisites, environment, ordered steps, expected results, verification and likely troubleshooting. Plan a testable procedure before committing to claims. Link optional background rather than burying the steps under it.
- **Comparison or alternatives:** reader decision, fair selection criteria, compared entities, a summary table, comparable evidence for each option, best-fit scenarios and limitations. Plan how volatile facts such as pricing will be dated. Do not select criteria solely to make our product win.
- **Explainer or guide:** direct answer, essential concepts, a concrete example, important distinctions and next steps. Broader coverage is useful only when it serves the question; a glossary paragraph is not automatically a separate article.
- **Case study:** starting situation, constraints, intervention, observed results, measurement basis and lessons. Identify permission and evidence needs; do not invent quotes or attribute outcomes to the intervention without support.
- **Refresh:** existing URL, reason for change, sections to retain, specific changes, new proof and expected reader benefit. Preserve the page's identity and approved material outside the scope.

These shapes complement the applicable owner playbook, not replace it. Useful defaults are to settle the reader promise before polishing the title, identify hard-to-obtain proof early, and keep the outline flexible enough for discoveries during writing. If research undermines the proposed answer, revise the brief rather than force evidence to fit it.

## Tools and integrations
Existing knowledge and research notes provide the foundation. Use connected search or page-reading tools when a claim or angle needs further investigation. Store the brief with the existing content record so it remains connected to feedback and the eventual draft.

## Useful output
An understandable proposed assignment that the owner can discuss and approve. It should communicate the intended outcome, angle and important evidence, not become a rigid document completed for its own sake. Use the detail necessary for this piece; leave room for good writing decisions during production.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Read the selected opportunity from its plan/Discovery, linked research and current Knowledge/voice notes. Link those inputs in the brief so the writer can revisit the reasoning.

For production-owned work, use agent-files/02-pipeline/<slug>/brief.md. For app-owned work, use agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/content/<slug>/brief.md with existing content identity, frontmatter and related-record links. Determine which location owns the item; do not create both. Draft, feedback and assets belong beside the same brief. Keep approval references and feedback attached to the relevant version through the existing request procedure. Link raw research where it lives. Update agent-files/INDEX.md for durable additions; label recovery snapshots as archives.
